title: Right now: estar + gerund
why: This lesson opens the unit on the present in motion: estar + gerund for what's happening right now, the handful of irregular gerunds, and seguir + gerund. It rounds out the simple present you've used since the start and sets up the near future with ir a + infinitive.

Estoy trabajando: what's happening right now

To say “I'm working,” Spanish uses estar + gerund: Estoy trabajando. Good news: this works just like the English “be + -ing.” Whenever you talk about what's going on at this very moment, this is the form to use. Just remember that the “be” here is always the verb for states and location, never the one for identity.

Forming the gerund

Take off the infinitive ending and add -ando for -ar verbs, -iendo for -er and -ir verbs. That's the Spanish “-ing.” The gerund never changes: no gender, no number.

InfinitiveStemGerund
hablarhabl-hablando
trabajartrabaj-trabajando
comercom-comiendo
hacerhac-haciendo
escribirescrib-escribiendo
salirsal-saliendo

Estar is conjugated, the gerund stays the same

PersonestarExample
yoestoyestoy hablando
túestásestás comiendo
él, ella, ustedestáestá escribiendo
nosotros, nosotrasestamosestamos cenando
vosotros, vosotrasestáisestáis haciendo
ellos, ellas, ustedesestánestán saliendo
¿Qué estás haciendo? — Estoy cocinando.What are you doing? — I'm cooking.

Unlike the English “-ing” form, the Spanish gerund is never used as a noun (“swimming is fun”) or as an adjective (“a sleeping baby”). Here, it always goes with estar (or seguir, below). And don't forget the accents on estás, está, estáis, están.

", "

Irregular gerunds

There aren't many, and they follow two simple rules.

1. -yendo after a vowel

When the stem ends in a vowel, -iendo becomes -yendo: an i between two vowels is written y.

InfinitiveGerund
leerleyendo
oíroyendo
traertrayendo
iryendo

2. Stem-changing -ir verbs

The -ir verbs that change their vowel in the present also change it in the gerund, but in a smaller step: e → i and o → u.

InfinitiveGerund
pedir (pido)pidiendo
decir (digo)diciendo
repetir (repito)repitiendo
servir (sirvo)sirviendo
seguir (sigo)siguiendo
vestirse (me visto)vistiéndose
preferir (prefiero)prefiriendo
dormir (duermo)durmiendo

Stem-changing -ar and -er verbs stay regular: pensar → pensando, volver → volviendo, empezar → empezando.

With a reflexive verb

The pronoun goes before estar: Me estoy duchando. You can also attach it to the end of the gerund, with a written accent to keep the stress in place: Estoy duchándome. Both are correct; the first is the simpler one.

Los niños se están vistiendo y el bebé está durmiendo.The kids are getting dressed and the baby is sleeping.

Learn three gerunds that come up all the time: leyendo, durmiendo, diciendo. ¿Qué estás diciendo? = What are you saying? What are you talking about?

", "

Simple present or estar + gerund?

The simple present describes a habit or a general truth; estar + gerund describes an action in progress, or a temporary situation. It's the same distinction English makes.

SpanishEnglish
Trabajo en un banco.I work at a bank (that's my job).
Hoy estoy trabajando en casa.Today I'm working from home (not usually).
Leo mucho.I read a lot (in general).
Estoy leyendo un libro muy bueno.I'm reading a really good book (right now).

For a quick question, you'll also hear the simple present: ¿Qué haces? (what are you up to?); but on the phone, to find out what someone is doing at this very moment, ¿Qué estás haciendo? is very natural.

Here's where English and Spanish part ways: this form isn't used with ser, tener or estar itself: Estoy en casa, Tengo hambre. With ir and venir, Spanish prefers the simple present, where English uses “-ing”: Ya voy (I'm coming!). And an English “-ing” for a future plan (“I'm leaving tomorrow”) is never the -ndo form in Spanish.

Seguir + gerund: “still,” “keep on”

Seguir (sigo, sigues, sigue, seguimos, seguís, siguen) + gerund says that an action is continuing. English says “still” or “keep (on) doing.”

Sigo estudiando español.I'm still studying Spanish.
¿Sigues viviendo en Sevilla?Do you still live in Seville?

After seguir, never an infinitive and never an “a”: Sigo trabajando, not “sigo a trabajar” or “sigo trabajar.” Think of English “keep working,” with the “-ing.”
